Accusative case.fact: In grammar, the accusative case (abbreviated acc) of a noun is the grammatical case used to receive the direct object of a transitive verb. In the English language, the only words that occur in the accusative case are pronouns: "me", "him", "her", "us", "whom", and "them".

Accusative case.subject: Indian Languages
Accusative case.question: For compound direct objects, it would be, e.g., "_____ invited me and her to the party"
Accusative case.fact: For example, the pronoun she, as the subject of a clause, is in the nominative case ("She wrote a book"); but if the pronoun is instead the object of the verb, it is in the accusative case and she becomes her ("Fred greeted her"). For compound direct objects, it would be, e.g., "Fred invited me and her to the party".

Accusative case.subject: Indian Languages
Accusative case.question: It is usually combined with the nominative case (for example in _____)
Accusative case.fact: It is usually combined with the nominative case (for example in Latin). The English term, "accusative", derives from the Latin accusativus, which, in turn, is a translation of the Greek αἰτιατική.

For example, in German, "the dog" is der Hund.
